This appeal is preferred by the State against the judgment of acquittal rendered by the Court of the V Additional District and Sessions Judge, Belagavi, in S.C. No.327/2014 dated 24th April, 2019,
wherein the accused have been acquitted for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.

3. The factual matrix of the case are as under:
In sum and substance, the prosecution case is that, the respondent accused No.1 married Seema on 19.11.2009 and after the marriage of Seema, the accused persons being the husband, mother-in-law and father-in-law started harassing her stating that she is not doing work properly, she is not cleaning and for no reason they started harassing her mentally and physically.

Seema unable to tolerate the mental and physical harassment of the accused persons that on 13.06.2014 between 09:30 a.m.
and 12:00 noon she committed suicide by hanging to the slab hook with the help of saree in the bedroom of the accused persons house and the accused persons have abetted her to commit suicide and thereby the accused persons have committed the above offences as alleged.

lodged a complaint before the Malmaruti Police Station against the accused persons by narrating the incident, that the accused persons have abetted her to commit suicide.
The same came to be registered in Crime No.134/2014.
Based on the complaint, a case was registered for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.

Subsequent to closure of the evidence for the prosecution, the accused were examined as required under Section 313 of Cr.P.C. for incriminating statements appeared against them.

The accused persons have denied the truth of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and the accused has produced marriage yadi as Ex.D1, but they did not come forward to adduce any defence evidence.
6. Subsequently, the trial Court heard the arguments advanced by the prosecution and the defence counsel.

On perusal of the entire evidence and the material documents, the accused have been acquitted for the offences punishable under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of IPC by alleging sound reasons.
It is this judgment, which is challenged under this appeal by urging various grounds.

7. Learned HCGP for the State during the course of his arguments has taken me through the evidence of PW.1- Shrishail Bagalkot, who is the father of the deceased Seema and also being the author of the complaint at Ex.P.1.

P.W.5 being the mother of the deceased, P.Ws.6 and 8 are the sisters of the deceased, P.W.9 is the uncle of the deceased, P.Ws.16 and 17 are the relatives of the deceased, who have consistently deposed before the Trial Court regarding the marriage talks and also performance of marriage on 19.11.2009 and also payment of Rs.1,50,000/- and 10 tholas of gold to his daughter and the respondent - accused No.1.

It is further submitted by the learned HCGP that all the above witnesses have stated about the frequent harassment both physically and mentally meted out to the deceased by the respondents - accused and all these witnesses have stated regarding continuous harassment and assault, by picking up quarrel with her, whereas these witnesses have advised respondents - accused and the deceased; but the deceased died on 13.06.2014 in the house of the respondents - accused by committing suicide by hanging due to physical and mental meted out to the deceased.

It is stated in their evidence which is consistent and corroborated to each other and nothing has been elicited in their cross- examination to disbelieve the truthful version of these material witnesses.
However, the Trial Court has erred in accepting the truthful version of the above said witnesses.

It is further stated that the Trial Court without proper appreciation of the evidence of the prosecution witnesses on its proper perspective has erroneously acquitted the respondents - accused, which is perverse and also miscarriage of justice.

However, the criminal law was set into motion based upon the complaint filed by P.W.1, the father of the deceased Seema and the same has been seen in the evidence of the witnesses namely P.Ws.1, 6, 8 and 9 and they are the witnesses on the part of the prosecution and also material witnesses, but in the evidence of these witnesses there are lot of improvements from time to time which is not at all the case of the prosecution and also the witnesses differs from person to person regarding the case of the prosecution, which creates doubt in the mind of the Court.
13. However, the prosecution case rests on the circumstantial evidence.

The law with regard to conviction on the basis of circumstantial evidence has very well been - 11 - crystallized in the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs. State of Maharashtra reported in (1984) 4 SCC 116, wherein it has held as under;
"152.

sentences.text: Before discussing the cases relied upon by the High Court we would like to cite a few decisions on the nature, character and essential proof required in a criminal case which rests on circumstantial evidence alone.

The most fundamental and basic decision of this Court is Hanumant v. State of Madhya Pradesh [AIR 1952 SC 343 :
1952 SCR 1091 : 1953 Cri LJ 129] .

and Ramgopal v. State of Maharashtra [(1972) 4 SCC 625: AIR 1972 SC 656].

It may be useful to extract what Mahajan, J. has laid down in Hanumant case [AIR 1952 SC 343 : 1952 SCR 1091 : 1953 Cri LJ 129] :
"It is well to remember that in in cases where the evidence is of a circumstantial nature, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should in the first instance be fully established, and all the facts so established should be State Of Karnataka vs Ravichandra Shivanand Gadad on 20 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180819066/

sentences.text: Again, the circum stances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency and they should be such as to exclude every hypothesis but the one proposed to be proved.

In other words, there must be a chain of evidence so far complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and it must be such as to show that within all human probability the act must have been done by the accused."

153. A close analysis of this decision would show that the following conditions must be fulfilled before a case against an accused can be said to be fully established:
(1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.

It may be noted here that this Court indicated that the circumstances concerned "must or should"
and not "may be" established.

There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between "may be proved" and "must be or should be proved" as was held by this Court in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra [(1973) 2 SCC 793 : 1973 SCC (Cri) 1033 : 1973 Crl LJ 1783] where the observations were made : [SCC para 19,
p. 807 :
SCC (Cri) p. 1047]
- 13 - "Certainly, it is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict and the mental distance between 'may be' and 'must be' is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions."
(2) the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused,
that is to say, they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty, (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency, (4) they should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved, and (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
154.

sentences.text: . This Court, therefore, has in no way departed from the five conditions laid down in - 14 - Hanumant's case (supra).

Unfortunately, however, the High Court also seems to have misconstrued this decision and used the so-called false defence put up by the appellant as one of the additional circumstances connected with the chain.
There is a vital difference between an incomplete chain of circumstances and a circumstance which, after the chain is complete, is added to it merely to reinforce the conclusion of the court.

Where the prosecution is unable to prove any of the essential principles laid down in Hanumant's case, the High Court cannot supply the weakness or the lacuna by taking aid of or recourse to a false defence or a false plea.
We are, therefore, unable to accept the argument of the Additional Solicitor-General.

162. Moreover, in M.G. Agarwal's case (supra) this Court while reiterating the principles enunciated in Hanumant's case observed thus:
"If the circumstances proved in the case are consistent either with the innocence of the accused or with his guilt, then the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt."

In Shankarlal's (supra) this Court reiterated the same view thus:
"Legal principles are not magic incantations and their importance lies more in their application to - 15 - a given set of facts than in their recital in the judgment".
163.
We then pass on to another important point which seems to have been completely missed by the High Court.

It is well settled that where on the evidence two possibilities are available or open,
one which goes in favour of the prosecution and the other which benefits an accused, the accused is undoubtedly entitled to the benefit of doubt.
In Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh,(l) this Court made the following observations:

"Another golden thread which runs through the web of the administration of justice in criminal cases is that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in the case one pointing to the guilt of the accused and the other to his innocence, the view which is favourable to the accused should be adopted This principle has a special relevance in cases where in the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence."
14.

sentences.text: This Court has held that there has to be a chain of evidence so complete so as not to leave any reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
It has been held that the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency.
This Court has held that the circumstances should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.
It has been held that the accused 'must be' and not merely 'may be' guilty before a Court can convict.
20. It is settled law that the suspicion, however strong it may be, cannot take the place of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
An accused cannot be convicted on the ground of suspicion, no matter how strong it is.
An accused is presumed to be innocent unless proved guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

i.e., the guilt of the accused.
In that view of the matter, we find that the judgment and order of the learned Sessions Judge and that of the High Court are not sustainable."

It is now well settled that the power of an appellate Court to review evidence in appeals against acquittal is as extensive as its powers in appeals against convictions, but that power is with a note of caution that the appellate Court should be slow in interfering with the orders of acquittal unless there are compelling reasons to do so.

This Court has held that the circumstances should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.

guilty before a Court can convict.
17. It is settled law
that the suspicion, however strong it may be, cannot take the place of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
An accused cannot be convicted on the ground of suspicion, no matter how so strong it is.
An accused is presumed to be innocent unless proved guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.
In the present case, I find that the prosecution has failure to establish the chain of events which can be said to exclusively lead to the one and only conclusion, i.e., the guilt of the accused.

19. However, the contention taken by the learned HCGP regarding non consideration of Exs.P18 and 19, that the concerned witnesses have turned hostile for seizing the said documents and the Trial Court has mentioned that the said document is not containing the date, time and place and during the course of investigation, the said document was not readily available with them as the Police had insisted the complainant to produce the same later and the same was produced at a later stage.

Therefore, it is said that the trial Court has rightly come to the conclusion by assigning sound reasons that the prosecution did not produce any cogent, consistent and acceptable evidence to probabalize the accusation that the accused had abetted Seema to commit suicide by hanging herself.

20. Therefore, this appeal does not call for any interference in the judgment of acquittal rendered by the Trial Court in S.C. No.327/2014 for the offences charged against - 20 - them under Sections 498A and 306 read with Section 34 of IPC.
Accordingly, the trial Court was right in coming to the conclusion by assigning sound reasoning that the accused deserve acquittal.

It is well settled that where on the evidence two possibilities are available or open,
one which goes in favour of the prosecution and the other which benefits an accused, the accused is undoubtedly entitled to the benefit of doubt.
It is now well settled that the power of an appellate Court to review evidence in appeals against acquittal is as extensive as its powers in appeals against convictions, but that power is with a note of caution that the appellate Court should be slow in interfering with the orders of acquittal unless there are compelling reasons to do so.

An accused cannot be convicted on the ground of suspicion, no matter how so strong it is.
An accused is presumed to be innocent unless proved guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

opennyai_summary.decision:
21. Therefore, in this appeal, I do not find any infirmity, perversity, absurdity and does not call for any interference with the acquittal judgment.
Consequently, the appeal deserves to be dismissed.
Accordingly, I proceed to pass the following order.
The appeal filed by the appellant-State under Sections 378(1) and (3) of Cr.P.C. is hereby dismissed.
Consequently, the judgment of acquittal rendered by the Trial Court in S.C. No.327/2014 dated 24th April, 2019 is hereby confirmed.
